impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for broad method-of-treatment claims requires the patent specification to enable the full scope of the functionally-defined genus of antibodies recited in the claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache using anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding sustains overly broad claims that undermine medical innovation and conflicts with Supreme Court enablement precedent. The denial leaves in place a panel ruling that could permit broad genus claims in biologic/antibody patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Originator pharmaceutical and biotech companies benefit from the ability to obtain and enforce broad method-of-treatment claims covering a genus of biologic molecules, strengthening patent portfolios around antibody therapeutics.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face broader patent barriers to entry, and competitors developing alternative antibodies within a claimed genus may face infringement risk from expansive method claims.

impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether, under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2), a reference patent's entitlement to the filing date of its provisional application requires that at least one claim of the non-provisional patent be supported by the provisional's written description, as held in Dynamic Drinkware for pre-AIA law.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination and remanded, addressing whether the Board correctly applied its Penumbra framework instead of Dynamic Drinkware to determine a reference's prior art date under AIA § 102(d)(2). The court's resolution of this question will clarify what is required for a patent reference to claim an earlier provisional filing date as prior art in IPR proceedings under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners may benefit from a narrower standard for when competitor patents qualify as prior art, potentially shielding patents from IPR challenges based on references with weak provisional application support.
impacts.negativeImplications: IPR petitioners and companies seeking to challenge patents face uncertainty about the prior art status of references with provisional applications, potentially limiting the prior art available in invalidity challenges.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents sufficient to allow the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to an enforcement-focused business model triggered a termination clause.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, granting standing to sue without joining the university. The court also held that TexasLDPC's pivot to patent enforcement did not constitute cessation of business operations triggering termination of the license agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from confirmation that broadly drafted exclusive licenses can confer standing to sue independently, and that shifting to an enforcement model does not necessarily terminate such licenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense of requiring joinder of the patent owner, and face litigation from exclusive licensees operating as enforcement-focused entities.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding the trade secret plaintiff's damages expert and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of proprietary automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of breach of contract damages, reinstating the jury's award. The decision affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret owners benefit from broader latitude in presenting damages models and from judicial respect for jury verdicts on contract damages, strengthening enforcement of IP licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology licensees face expanded exposure to trade secret misappropriation claims and damages when developing competing products after licensing relationships end, with courts more willing to allow alternative damages theories to reach the jury.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL of non-infringement and on damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the eligibility determination for some asserted claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement, and affirmed the damages award in a case involving communication system patents used in television broadcasting. The split ruling provides important guidance on how § 101 eligibility applies to claims involving mathematical optimization applied to specific technical systems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications and signal processing technology receive confirmation that claims tied to specific technical implementations of mathematical concepts can survive § 101 challenges, and that jury damages awards will be upheld on appeal.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology implementers incorporating industry-standard communication protocols face continued patent infringement exposure, with some eligibility challenges failing on appeal.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess ordinary observer test for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences between designs rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality determinations in design patent claim construction present factual questions for the jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing on a design patent infringement case, with significant disagreement among the judges. The concurrence defended the existing Egyptian Goddess framework, while Chief Judge Moore's dissent argued the framework improperly shifts focus to differences and allows courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment without adequate examination of prior art and functionality issues that should go to a jury.
impacts.positiveImplications: Design patent defendants benefit from the maintained framework that permits summary judgment of non-infringement when designs are sufficiently distinct, providing earlier and less costly resolution of design patent disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a framework that critics argue is biased toward finding non-infringement, with four judges signaling that the current test may be improperly applied to deny jury consideration of infringement.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's contingent payment provision tied to the outcome of a patent reexamination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a contract interpretation dispute arising from a patent settlement agreement, because the question of whether asserted claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination was a state law contract issue that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question. The case was transferred to the Fifth Circuit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties structuring patent settlements with contingent payments tied to PTO proceedings gain clarity that disputes over such provisions may be adjudicated in regional circuits rather than the Federal Circuit, potentially providing more favorable forums.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies may face uncertainty about which appellate court will resolve patent settlement disputes, and the ruling may complicate forum selection when drafting settlement agreements with patent-related contingencies.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient reasoning when denying motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 in a case where the patentee asserted claims despite related applications being rejected under § 101 post-Alice.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and attorneys' fees, holding that the district court failed to provide sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that brought infringement claims despite multiple related applications having been rejected under § 101 after Alice and a related patent being invalidated in another district court.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from heightened scrutiny of fee-shifting denials, potentially deterring assertion of patents with significant § 101 vulnerability and ensuring district courts adequately justify decisions not to award fees in exceptional cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk that pursuing infringement claims involving patents related to § 101-rejected applications could result in fee-shifting, chilling legitimate patent enforcement in uncertain eligibility areas.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly awarded attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and sanctions under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 against the patentee and its counsel for pursuing a frivolous patent infringement claim, and whether counsel's failure to separately appeal bars appellate review of personal sanctions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of the patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, upheld the finding that the case was exceptional under § 285, and affirmed the award of over $207,000 in attorneys' fees. The court also addressed the procedural requirements for counsel to independently appeal personal sanctions orders.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases benefit from robust fee-shifting mechanisms that deter frivolous patent assertions, particularly where patentees file inadequate complaints and seek pre-suit damages without proper notice allegations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face significant financial risk when filing infringement suits with deficient pleadings, with both entity and counsel potentially held jointly and severally liable for the defendant's fees.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit may affirm a judgment of patent invalidity on the alternative ground of lack of enablement when the district court ruled solely on indefiniteness grounds, and whether claims reciting transmission of signals 'over air' with impedance matching are enabled.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on the alternative ground of lack of enablement. The court held that the patent's claims, which broadly recited transmitting signals over air using a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air, were not enabled because the specification did not teach how to practice the full scope of the claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringement benefit from the Federal Circuit's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not reached by the district court, providing more efficient resolution of patent disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders risk invalidation on grounds not fully litigated below, and must ensure claims are supported by adequate enablement disclosure across their full scope.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in a sunset review of an antidumping duty order within 15 days of the notice of initiation conflicts with the governing statute.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in sunset reviews of antidumping duty orders is a permissible exercise of the agency's delegated authority. The court found the statute silent on the filing deadline and upheld Commerce's regulatory requirement as the product of reasoned decisionmaking.
impacts.positiveImplications: Foreign exporters and importers benefit from clear procedural deadlines that could result in revocation of antidumping duty orders if domestic producers fail to timely participate in sunset reviews.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic manufacturers face the risk of losing antidumping protection if they fail to meet Commerce's 15-day participation deadline, even though the statute itself imposes no express deadline.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the term 'internal diameter' in oil and gas tool patent claims and whether the jury's findings of infringement and validity were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's judgment finding infringement of a patent related to casing flotation tools used in oil and gas wellbores. The case turned on the construction of 'internal diameter' in the patent claims, with significant implications for how dimensional terms in mechanical patents are interpreted.
impacts.positiveImplications: Oil and gas equipment manufacturers benefit from careful judicial scrutiny of claim construction for mechanical patent terms, potentially narrowing the scope of competitor patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the oil and gas industry face the risk that broadly drafted dimensional claim terms may be construed more narrowly on appeal, undermining infringement findings.
